reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / NCCN & genetics references
clinicalPearls: The most common hereditary colorectal cancer syndrome, caused by germline variants in a DNA mismatch repair gene (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2) or by EPCAM deletions that silence MSH2, inherited autosomal dominantly
Confers high lifetime risk of colorectal cancer, typically with earlier onset than sporadic disease and a predilection for the right (proximal) colon
Endometrial cancer is the second commonest malignancy and may be the sentinel (first) cancer in affected women
Extracolonic risks include ovarian, gastric, small bowel, urothelial, pancreatic, biliary, and brain tumours (Turcot phenotype) and sebaceous skin neoplasms (Muir-Torre phenotype)
Tumours characteristically show microsatellite instability and loss of mismatch repair protein staining on immunohistochemistry, which guides germline testing
Colonoscopic surveillance beginning at a young age with short screening intervals reduces colorectal cancer incidence and mortality because adenomas can progress rapidly
Risk-reducing hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy are discussed for women once childbearing is complete
Universal tumour screening of colorectal and endometrial cancers for mismatch repair deficiency helps identify previously undiagnosed families
reference.pathophysiology: The DNA mismatch repair system corrects base-base mismatches and small insertion-deletion loops arising during replication. A germline loss-of-function variant in a mismatch repair gene, followed by somatic inactivation of the second allele, leaves cells unable to repair these errors. Repetitive microsatellite sequences are especially vulnerable, producing microsatellite instability and a rapidly accumulating mutational burden that accelerates the adenoma-to-carcinoma sequence and drives the broad tumour spectrum. The resulting high neoantigen load also makes these tumours responsive to immune checkpoint inhibition.
additionalDifferentials: Familial adenomatous polyposis and attenuated FAP
Familial colorectal cancer type X without mismatch repair deficiency
Sporadic microsatellite-unstable colorectal cancer from MLH1 promoter hypermethylation
Other hereditary gastrointestinal cancer predisposition syndromes
additionalInvestigations: Tumour testing with mismatch repair immunohistochemistry and microsatellite instability analysis
BRAF mutation and MLH1 promoter methylation testing to distinguish sporadic from hereditary MLH1 loss
Germline sequencing and deletion/duplication analysis of mismatch repair genes and EPCAM with genetic counselling
Regular colonoscopy with short intervals as the core surveillance modality
Gynaecological assessment, and consideration of upper gastrointestinal and urinary tract surveillance based on gene and family history
redFlags: Colorectal or endometrial cancer diagnosed at an unusually young age
Multiple Lynch-associated cancers in one individual or clustering across close relatives
Right-sided colorectal tumour with mismatch repair-deficient histology
Rapid progression of colonic neoplasia between screening intervals
reference.prognosis: Stage for stage, mismatch repair-deficient colorectal cancers may carry a relatively favourable prognosis and respond well to immunotherapy, but the lifetime and metachronous cancer risk is substantial. Intensive colonoscopic surveillance markedly reduces colorectal cancer mortality, and outcomes depend on adherence to screening and risk-reducing measures.
pitfalls: Relying on clinical family-history criteria alone and missing families that do not meet them; universal tumour screening captures more cases
Interpreting MLH1 protein loss as hereditary without excluding sporadic promoter hypermethylation
Extending colonoscopy intervals as for average-risk patients, allowing interval cancers
Neglecting endometrial and other extracolonic surveillance and risk-reducing surgery options
